modules.title: What Is AI and Machine Learning?
modules.summary: How computers learn patterns from data, and how that is different from following rules.

lessons.title: Rules vs. Learning
lessons.body:
Traditional programs follow exact instructions written by people: if this, then that. Artificial intelligence works differently. A machine-learning model is shown many examples — thousands of photos of cats and dogs, for instance — and it gradually adjusts itself until it can tell them apart on its own.

This matters for you as a student because AI systems are only as good as the examples they learned from. If a model has never seen a husky in the snow, it might call it a wolf. When you use AI tools at school, remember: they are pattern-matchers, not thinkers. They can be very useful, but they can also be confidently wrong.

Canada's National AI Literacy Initiative, launched in September 2026 with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii), begins with exactly this idea — understanding how AI and machine learning actually work.
lessons.activity: Sort 10 everyday tasks into 'rules' (a calculator, a traffic light) or 'learning' (spam filter, voice assistant). Explain one choice to a partner.

quiz.q: A machine-learning model gets better mainly by…
Why might an AI misidentify a husky as a wolf?

lessons.title: Where Does Training Data Come From?
lessons.body:
Every AI system starts with data: text from websites, photos people uploaded, recordings of speech. Companies collect enormous amounts of it. Some data is public, some is licensed, and some is gathered in ways that raise fair questions about consent and copyright.

Ask three questions about any AI tool: Whose data trained it? Who is represented — and who is missing? Who benefits? These questions connect directly to Canadian conversations about privacy and Indigenous data sovereignty, which you will explore in later modules.
lessons.activity: Pick an AI app you use. Find its privacy policy and identify one sentence about how your data is used.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three data questions?
options: How many pixels does it have?

modules.title: Generative AI & Cognitive Offloading
modules.summary: What chatbots and image generators really do, and how to use them without letting your brain go on autopilot.

lessons.title: How Chatbots Predict Words
lessons.body:
A large language model does not look up answers in a database. It predicts the most likely next word, again and again, based on patterns in the text it was trained on. That is why it can write a fluent paragraph about almost anything — and why it can invent a fake book title or a wrong date that sounds completely real. Researchers call these 'hallucinations'.

The practical rule: treat AI output like a first draft from a very confident stranger. Verify names, numbers, quotes, and sources before you rely on them. Educators across Canada — from B.C. to New Brunswick — now teach students to check AI results for bias, mistakes, and copyright issues.
lessons.activity: Ask an approved chatbot for three facts about your town. Verify each with a trusted source. Mark them true, false, or partly true.

lessons.title: Keep Your Brain in the Loop
lessons.body:
Cognitive offloading means handing a mental task to a tool — like using a calculator or a GPS. It is not always bad. But if you offload the thinking you are supposed to be practising, you never build the skill. Research on learning shows that struggling with a problem first, then getting feedback, leads to deeper understanding than reading a finished answer.

A healthy pattern: attempt first, use AI to compare or critique, then revise in your own words. Many Canadian schools describe this as 'AI as a study partner, not a ghost-writer'. Your teacher decides which stages of an assignment allow AI help; the AI-use disclosure tools in this platform help you make that visible.
lessons.activity: Write a paragraph on a topic first. Then ask AI for feedback only. Highlight what you changed and why.

quiz.q: The recommended order for using AI on homework is…

modules.title: Bias, Deepfakes & Misinformation
modules.summary: Spot unfair patterns in AI, recognise synthetic media, and build habits of verification.

lessons.title: Where Bias Comes From
lessons.body:
AI learns from the world as it was recorded, and the record is uneven. If historical hiring data favoured one group, a hiring model may too. If image datasets contain few pictures of northern or Indigenous communities, the model will describe them poorly. Bias is not a bug you can simply delete; it is a mirror of the data and the choices designers made.

As a critical user, look for: who is shown, who is stereotyped, whose language is handled well. Report unfair results to your teacher — most Canadian districts now ask students to flag bias as part of responsible use.
lessons.activity: Ask an image generator for 'a scientist' five times. Tally who appears. Discuss what the pattern tells you about the training data.

options: Uneven training data and design choices

lessons.title: Deepfakes and Digital Forensics
lessons.body:
Generative AI can clone a voice from a few seconds of audio and swap faces in video. Some uses are creative and legal; others are harassment or fraud. Sharing intimate deepfakes of classmates is a crime in Canada.

Detection habits: check the source account, look for mismatched lighting or lip-sync, reverse-image-search, and pause before sharing anything designed to make you angry. When in doubt, ask a trusted adult — and never create synthetic media of a real person without their consent.
lessons.activity: Compare a real and an AI-generated news clip (teacher-provided). List three clues that helped you decide.

quiz.q: Before sharing a shocking video you should…

modules.title: Privacy & Your Data
modules.summary: Why schools approve specific tools, what 'enterprise data protection' means, and how to protect yourself online.

lessons.title: Why Only Approved Tools?
lessons.body:
Most AI apps set a minimum age of 13 and collect personal information. Schools in Canada must follow provincial privacy laws for students, so they vet tools first. For example, the Vancouver School Board approved Microsoft Copilot with Enterprise Data Protection, meaning student prompts are not used to train the public model and stay inside the district's account.

Using an unapproved AI tool for schoolwork can expose your data — and may break your school's acceptable-use policy. Ask your teacher which tools are cleared, and never type personal details (full name, address, health info) into any AI chat.
lessons.activity: List the AI tools approved by your school. For each, write one thing it may do with your data.

options: Prompts stay within the organisation's account

modules.title: Academic Integrity in the AI Era
modules.summary: Where the line is between help and cheating, how to disclose AI use, and how to cite it.

lessons.title: Disclose, Don't Disguise
lessons.body:
Submitting AI-generated work as your own is treated as plagiarism in Canadian schools. But using AI to brainstorm, check grammar, or explain a concept is often allowed — if your teacher permits it and you say so. Many schools now use a traffic-light system: green (AI encouraged), yellow (AI for specific stages, must be disclosed), red (no AI).

A good disclosure statement names the tool, what you used it for, and what you changed. Example: 'I used Copilot to suggest an outline; all writing and sources are my own.' Use the AI-Use Statement Generator in the Teacher Hub to practise.
lessons.activity: Draft an AI-use statement for your last assignment, real or hypothetical, using the generator.

options: AI allowed for specific stages, with disclosure

modules.title: Indigenous Data Sovereignty
modules.summary: The OCAP® principles and why communities should govern data about themselves — including in AI.

lessons.title: Ownership, Control, Access, Possession
lessons.body:
Indigenous data sovereignty is the right of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples to govern the collection, ownership and use of data about their communities, lands, languages and knowledge. The First Nations principles of OCAP® — Ownership, Control, Access and Possession — are one widely used framework in Canada.

Why does this matter for AI? Models are trained on scraped data that may include Indigenous languages, stories and images taken without consent. Canada's national educator course includes this topic because responsible AI in classrooms must respect these rights. As a learner, ask: was this knowledge shared with permission, and who decides how it is used?
lessons.activity: Research one Indigenous-led language or data project in Canada. Present how it applies OCAP® principles.

modules.title: Responsible Use in the Classroom
modules.summary: Acceptable-use policies, digital wellbeing, and a checklist you can apply to any AI task.

lessons.title: The 5-Question Checklist
lessons.body:
Before using AI for any school task, run the checklist: 1) Am I allowed? (Check the assignment's colour.) 2) Is this tool approved by my school? 3) Am I sharing private data? 4) Will I verify the output? 5) Will I disclose how I used it?

If any answer is 'no' or 'not sure', stop and ask. These five questions summarise the acceptable-use rules found in Canadian school districts from B.C. to Manitoba to New Brunswick.
lessons.activity: Create a poster of the 5-Question Checklist for your classroom.

quiz.q: If you're not sure whether AI is allowed, you should…

modules.title: Future-Ready: Careers & Creativity with AI
modules.summary: How AI is changing jobs in Canada, and the durable human skills that matter more than ever.

lessons.title: Working Alongside AI
lessons.body:
AI is reshaping work in Canada — from agriculture in Saskatchewan to film in Vancouver to health research in Toronto. Most jobs will not disappear, but they will change: people who can direct, evaluate and improve AI output will be in demand. Programs like CanCode ($30 million, 2026–2028, reaching 1.1 million students and 76,000 teachers) exist to make sure every young Canadian gets this chance.

The skills that hold their value are human ones: asking good questions, judging evidence, collaborating across cultures and languages, and creating things that matter to your community. Being bilingual — in English, French, Chinese or any language — is itself a superpower in a world of global AI tools.
lessons.activity: Interview a family member about how technology changed their job. Predict one way AI might change a career you're interested in.

quiz.q: Which skill becomes MORE valuable as AI spreads?
options: Judging evidence and asking good questions
